[[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Tim Sheehy]] won his first term in office, defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] three-term incumbent [[Jon Tester]]. Despite the state's heavy partisan lean in favor of the Republican Party, Tester remained popular among his constituents. Because of this and Montana's historical inclination to [[Split-ticket voting|ticket-split]], the race was considered to be competitive. Early polling showed Tester to be leading or nearly even, but Sheehy later gained an edge. Tester was widely seen as being the most vulnerable incumbent running for re-election, due to Montana's strong Republican lean and the decline of [[split-ticket voting]].{{Cite web|url=https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/will-a-generic-republican-beat-tester-and-flip-the-senate.html|title=Will a Generic Republican Beat Tester and Flip the Senate?|first1=Ed|last1=Kilgore|website=New York Magazine|date=October 4, 2024|access-date=October 4, 2024}} Tester, a renowned [[Centrism in the United States|centrist]] liberal, was first elected in [[2006 United States Senate election in Montana|2006]], when he narrowly defeated incumbent Republican senator [[Conrad Burns]], and was reelected in [[2012 United States Senate election in Montana|2012]] and [[2018 United States Senate election in Montana|2018]]. However, come Election Day in 2024, his vulnerability came to fruition as he lost his bid for a fourth term to Tim Sheehy by around 7.1 percentage points. Sheehy received roughly 52.6% of the statewide vote to Tester's 45.5%. Despite his loss, Tester still vastly outperformed [[Kamala Harris]], who lost the state to [[Donald Trump]] in the concurrent presidential race by just under 20 percentage points. Tester also carried six counties that Trump concurrently won: [[Big Horn County, Montana|Big Horn]], [[Blaine County, Montana|Blaine]], [[Hill County, Montana|Hill]], [[Lewis and Clark County, Montana|Lewis and Clark]] ([[Helena, Montana|Helena]]), [[Roosevelt County, Montana|Roosevelt]], and [[Park County, Montana|Park]]. Tester received over 44,000 more raw votes than Harris, while Sheehy received over 32,000 fewer raw votes than Trump. Along with [[Bob Casey Jr.]] in [[2024 United States Senate election in Pennsylvania|Pennsylvania]] and [[Sherrod Brown]] in [[2024 United States Senate election in Ohio|Ohio]], Tester was one of three incumbent senators to lose re-election in 2024. All three were first elected in [[2006 United States Senate elections|2006]], defeating Republican incumbents, and won re-election in [[2012 United States Senate elections|2012]] and [[2018 United States Senate elections|2018]]. This race was one of two 2024 U.S. Senate races in which Democratic senators sought re-election in states where Republican [[Donald Trump]] won in both the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections, the other being Ohio. With Sheehy's victory, Republicans held both of Montana's Senate seats for the first time since 1911. {{TOC limit|3}} == Background == Montana has generally been considered a [[Red states and blue states|red state]] at the federal executive level, voting for Republican candidates in each presidential election starting in [[1996 United States presidential election in Montana|1996]], when [[Bob Dole]] beat [[Bill Clinton]] by nearly 3 percentage points in a three-way race with [[Ross Perot]]. Since then, GOP candidates have won the White House race in the state by double digits in every race except in [[2008 United States presidential election in Montana|2008]]. In the most recent presidential election, in [[2020 United States presidential election in Montana|2020]], [[Donald Trump]] beat [[Joe Biden]] in Montana by 56.92% to 40.55%. Republicans have also won all of the state's [[United States House of Representatives|U.S. House]] elections since 1996. Within this time frame, Democrats have been more successful in elections for state offices and the U.S. Senate, with its [[Governor of Montana|governorship]], [[Montana State Legislature|state legislature]], and Senate seats alternating between Democratic and Republican control. Leading up to the 2024 election, Republicans controlled both of Montana's U.S. House seats, the other U.S. Senate seat, the governorship, and had supermajority control of both houses of the state legislature.{{cn|date=February 2026}} Tester refused to endorse fellow Democrat [[Kamala Harris]] for president, a contributing factor towards the Senate race having been considered less nationalized. In 2012, the last election that featured Tester on the same ballot as the presidential election, Republican [[2012 United States presidential election in Montana|presidential candidate Mitt Romney won by 13.64%]], while [[2012 United States Senate election in Montana|Tester won by 3.72%]] without receiving a majority (50%) of the vote.{{cite news |last=Yokley |first=Eli |title=Red-State Voters Give Democrats Tester, Manchin Opposite Marks Ahead of 2024 |url=https://morningconsult.com/2023/04/19/joe-manchin-jon-tester-approval-rating/ |access-date=April 27, 2023 |work=[[Morning Consult]] |date=April 19, 2023}}{{cite news |last=Coleman |first=J. The bill's sponsor, Republican [[Greg Hertz]], said it would require the winner of the 2024 Senate race to receive a majority of the vote. Incumbent Democrat [[Jon Tester]] won with a plurality of the vote in his [[2006 United States Senate election in Montana|2006]] and [[2012 United States Senate election in Montana|2012]] Senate campaigns, though he won a majority in [[2018 United States Senate election in Montana|2018]]. Both Democrats and Libertarians alleged the bill was intended to prevent the Libertarian Party from placing a nominee on the general election ballot in the Senate race who could potentially [[spoiler effect|pull votes away]] from the Republican nominee, with Democratic state senator [[Ryan Lynch (politician)|Ryan Lynch]] calling it a "partisan power grab."{{cite news |first=Arren |last=Kimbel-Sannit |date=April 3, 2023 |url=https://montanafreepress.org/2023/04/03/bill-would-create-atop-two-primary-in-montanas-2024-u-s-senate-race/ |title=Senate passes bill creating top-two primary in Tester's 2024 U.S. Senate race}}{{Cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/2024-election-senate-montana-primary-tester-de0019352c2f1c1235739491e2553825|title=Republicans seek to change Montana primary to thwart Tester|date=April 5, 2023|website=AP News|access-date=August 6, 2023}} After the bill received backlash, Hertz introduced an amendment to make the use of a top-two primary for U.S. Senate elections permanent rather than sunsetting it after the 2024 race.{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/14/us/politics/montana-election-bill-senate-tester.html |title=Facing Tough Senate Race, Montana G.O.P.
